passage:
Akash: hey are you up
Jahnavi: yes what's up
Akash: someone in class called me "stick insect" today. I keep looking at my arms in the mirror and hating them
Jahnavi: that's a rubbish thing to say
Akash: and the guys on my feed all look like statues. I feel broken
Jahnavi: those pics are edited and lit and probably took ten takes
Jahnavi: also you're the one who cycled 12 km last weekend, remember? your legs did that
Akash: ...ok yes that was pretty good
Jahnavi: your body carries you around. it's not a photo
Akash: I'll try to remember that. thanks for staying up
Jahnavi: anytime. want to cycle on Sunday?

How does Akash feel about their body, and why?
qa.a: Akash feels ashamed and hurt about their body, hating their arms and feeling broken, because of the classmate's comment and the edited pictures on the feed.

qa.q: What reminders from Jahnavi could help Akash?
qa.a: That the pictures are edited and posed, and that Akash's body did something strong when it cycled 12 km. 🤍

qa.q: How might Jahnavi feel about being messaged late by Akash?
qa.a: Jahnavi seems caring and willing to stay up, which shows Jahnavi takes Akash's feelings seriously and wants Akash to feel less alone.

grounding: Shows a teen hating their body after a comment and edited pictures, and a friend pointing to editing and what the body does.

passage: Monday. After Mama Ji laughed at the wedding, 'Siddharth, you're thin as a broom,' Siddharth scrolled gym reels until midnight: perfect arms, shining abs. He wore two T-shirts to school the next day so nobody would see his shoulders. Thursday. His cousin Disha caught him frowning at his phone. She opened a photo editor and, in three swipes, made her own arms bigger and her waist smaller. 'Half those reels are lit, posed and edited like this,' she said. 'You're comparing yourself to a filter.' He stared at the screen for a long time. Two weeks later. Siddharth had joined the school swimming batch. Tired and dripping after his first full length without stopping, he caught sight of himself in the changing-room mirror and, for once, thought about what his shoulders had just done, not how they looked.

qa.q: What did Disha show Siddharth with the photo editor?
qa.a: In three swipes she made her own arms bigger and her waist smaller.

qa.q: Why did Siddharth wear two T-shirts to school?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and self-conscious about his thin shoulders after Mama Ji's joke and the reels.

qa.q: What helped Siddharth start to shift how he saw his body?
qa.a: Seeing how reels are edited, then swimming, which let him notice what his body can do rather than how it looks 💪

qa.q: How does Disha see Siddharth's scrolling?
qa.a: She sees him comparing himself to edited images, so she shows him the trick instead of just telling him he's fine.

grounding: Shows a teen ashamed of his body after a comment and online pictures, noticing the standard is edited and shifting focus to what his body does.

passage: Ritu, you think I didn't care about mirrors at your age? I was fourteen when my aunties started, at every function: 'Nirmala is getting so dark, so round, who will marry her?' The film posters outside Lakshmi Talkies showed heroines with skin like milk and waists like pencils, and I hated my arms, my face, everything. I stopped going to kho-kho practice so nobody would see me run. Then I got a holiday job at Venkat uncle's photo studio. One afternoon he showed me a heroine's photo before and after his brush: he lightened her skin, shaved her waist, erased a scar. 'Nobody looks like this, child. Not even her.' I went back to kho-kho that week. Those legs made me captain two years later. So when you tell me your photos online look wrong, listen to Nirmala Paati: ask what your body can do.

qa.q: What did Venkat uncle change in the heroine's photo?
qa.a: He lightened her skin, shaved her waist and erased a scar.

qa.q: What was Nirmala feeling when the aunties commented at functions?
qa.a: Nirmala felt ashamed and hurt, hating every part of that body, enough to quit kho-kho so nobody would watch.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed Nirmala's choice?
qa.a: Seeing the before-and-after photo at the studio showed the posters were edited, so going back to kho-kho made sense.

qa.q: How did Venkat uncle see the heroine's poster?
qa.a: He knew it was his own brushwork, not a real person, and wanted Nirmala to know nobody looks like that.

grounding: An elder's story of body shame from comments and retouched pictures, learning the standard was edited and focusing on what the body can do.
